claims.text: Introducing a minor fraction of Cu into a tungsten-based high-entropy alloy will improve heat-transfer capability.
Introducing Cu will preserve the alloy's structural integrity under plasma-facing reactor conditions.
The initial material can be a W-Ta-Cr-V high-entropy alloy or a similar tungsten-based composition.
The initial tungsten-based HEA currently serves as an intermediate layer between plasma-facing and cooling components.
The initial alloy has established mechanical integrity and moderate thermal conductivity.
The proposed intervention is to add approximately 5-10 at% Cu during alloy synthesis.
Suitable processing can produce a single-phase microstructure in the Cu-modified alloy.
Cu addition will yield a uniform single-phase solid solution containing coherent nanoscale features.
Grain size, phase stability, and precipitate coherence will be maintained despite Cu addition.
Copper has high intrinsic thermal conductivity.
Dispersed Cu in the HEA matrix will create additional electronic and phononic heat-conduction pathways.
Controlled Cu addition will not nucleate deleterious secondary phases.
The additional conduction pathways will increase overall heat transport.
The Cu-modified matrix will remain mechanically robust and irradiation resistant.
The Cu-modified alloy will have greater effective thermal conductivity than the unmodified control.
The Cu-modified alloy will show no significant loss of mechanical strength or structural stability under reactor-relevant conditions.
The enhancement is expected to persist during prolonged high-temperature, high-heat-flux, and potential irradiation exposure without phase segregation or mechanical weakening.

contradictions.description: The material is required to be a single-phase solid solution, yet the mediator invokes precipitate coherence. Distinct precipitates ordinarily imply an additional phase unless the term is intended to mean coherent compositional fluctuations rather than true precipitates.
